sections.title: Section A — Units I to IV (compulsory)
Section B1 — Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
Section B2 — Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Partner's loan to the firm
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about a loan given by a partner to the firm:
(A) A partner's loan is shown separately and is not added to his capital.
(B) In the absence of an agreement, interest on it is allowed at 6% p.a.
(C) Interest on the loan is a charge against profit.
(D) Interest on the loan is credited to the partner's Capital Account.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why:
(A) True — a loan is a separate liability (shown under liabilities), and it ranks ahead of capital on dissolution.
(B) True — Section 13(d) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.
(C) True — the interest is payable even if there is a loss.
(D) False — the interest is credited to the partner's LOAN Account (Interest on Loan A/c Dr.; To Partner's Loan A/c), not his Capital Account.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (D) all include the false statement (D).
Key point: Loan and its interest → Loan A/c; capital and appropriations → Capital/Current A/c.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Fixed capital method — partner's current account balance
questions.question: A's capital is fixed. His Current Account had an opening CREDIT balance of ₹10,000. During the year he was credited with interest on capital of ₹10,000 and his share of profit of ₹30,000. His drawings were ₹45,000, and interest on drawings was ₹1,500. The closing balance of his Current Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹3,500 (Cr.)
Step 1: Credits = Opening ₹10,000 + Interest on capital ₹10,000 + Share of profit ₹30,000 = ₹50,000
Step 2: Debits = Drawings ₹45,000 + Interest on drawings ₹1,500 = ₹46,500
Step 3: Closing balance = ₹50,000 − ₹46,500 = ₹3,500 credit
Common mistake: Treating interest on drawings as a credit gives ₹6,500 Cr. (A). Reversing the final balance gives (B). Ignoring the opening balance gives ₹6,500 Dr. (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — factors affecting
questions.question: Which of the following does NOT affect the goodwill of a firm?
options: D) Private assets of the partners
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Private assets of the partners
Why: Goodwill depends on the firm's ability to earn above-normal profits, which is shaped by its nature, location, management, market position and special advantages. The partners' personal property does not affect the firm's earning capacity.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are among the factors affecting goodwill that NCERT lists.
Key point: Goodwill depends on the earning power of the business, not on the partners' personal wealth.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Revaluation — gains and losses that cancel out
questions.question: At the time of reconstitution: the existing provision for doubtful debts of ₹5,000 on debtors of ₹80,000 is to be maintained at 5%; stock is to be increased by ₹6,000; and machinery of ₹70,000 is to be depreciated by 10%. The result of revaluation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Neither profit nor loss
Step 1: Required provision = 5% × ₹80,000 = ₹4,000; existing ₹5,000 → excess ₹1,000 written back (gain)
Step 2: Stock increase = ₹6,000 (gain)
Step 3: Depreciation on machinery = 10% × ₹70,000 = ₹7,000 (loss)
Step 4: Net = ₹1,000 + ₹6,000 − ₹7,000 = nil
Common mistake: Ignoring the machinery gives a profit of ₹7,000 (A). Ignoring the provision write-back gives a loss of ₹1,000 (B). Treating the provision change as a loss gives a loss of ₹2,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Realisation Account versus Revaluation Account
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Realisation Account is prepared only on dissolution of the firm.
(B) On dissolution of a partnership (reconstitution), a Revaluation Account is prepared instead.
(C) On dissolution of a firm, the Cash/Bank Account is closed last.
(D) On dissolution, partners' Current Accounts are transferred to the Realisation Account.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why:
(A) True — realisation means selling up the business, which happens only when the firm ends.
(B) True — on reconstitution the firm continues, so assets and liabilities are only revalued.
(C) True — the cash account is closed when the partners are finally paid.
(D) False — Current Account balances are transferred to the partners' CAPITAL Accounts, not to the Realisation Account.
Why not the others: Options (B), (C) and (D) all include the false statement (D).
Key point: Realisation A/c → only outside assets and liabilities.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — where each item is credited
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II on the admission of a new partner:

List-I (Item)
(A) Increase in the value of land
(B) General Reserve
(C) Premium for goodwill brought in by the new partner
(D) Cash brought in by the new partner as his capital

List-II (Credited to)
(I) The old partners' Capital Accounts directly, in the old ratio
(II) The Revaluation Account
(III) The new partner's Capital Account
(IV) The sacrificing partners' Capital Accounts

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why:
(A) A rise in asset value is a revaluation gain → Revaluation A/c (II); its balance later goes to the old partners.
(B) A reserve is transferred directly to the old partners in the old ratio → (I).
(C) The premium compensates the sacrificing partners → (IV).
(D) The capital brought belongs to the new partner → (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the land and reserve treatments; (C) swaps the premium and capital; (D) sends the land gain to the sacrificing partners.
Key point: Revaluation items pass through the Revaluation A/c; reserves go directly to capitals.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Re-issue of forfeited shares — working back to the number of shares
questions.question: 600 equity shares of ₹10 each, fully called up, on which ₹4 per share had been paid, were forfeited. Some of these shares were re-issued at ₹7 per share as fully paid. The amount transferred to Capital Reserve on the re-issue was ₹600. How many shares were re-issued?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 600
Step 1: Forfeited amount per share = ₹4
Step 2: Discount on re-issue per share = ₹10 − ₹7 = ₹3
Step 3: Surplus transferred to Capital Reserve per re-issued share = ₹4 − ₹3 = ₹1
Step 4: Number re-issued = ₹600 ÷ ₹1 = 600 shares (that is, all of them)
Common mistake: Dividing by the forfeited amount (₹4) gives 150 (A). Dividing by the discount (₹3) gives 200 (B). Dividing by ₹2 gives 300 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Calls in advance — interest and nature
questions.question:
Assertion (A): A company may pay interest on calls in advance.
Reason (R): Calls in advance is a liability of the company.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Interest may be paid on calls in advance because the company's Articles (Table F allows up to 12% p.a.) permit it, as compensation to the shareholder for paying early — so the Assertion is true. Calls in advance is indeed a liability until the call is made — so the Reason is true. But being a liability is about its PRESENTATION; the right to interest comes from the Articles, so the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
Why not the others: (A) wrongly links the two. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Interest on calls in advance → Articles (Table F); presentation → Other current liabilities.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Guarantee of profit — no deficiency arises
questions.question: In a firm of three partners sharing 3 : 2 : 1, the youngest partner C has been promised that his share of profit will never be less than ₹50,000; if it ever falls short, A alone will make up the difference. This year the firm earned ₹3,60,000. How much profit will be credited to A?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,80,000
Step 1: C's normal share = ₹3,60,000 × 1/6 = ₹60,000
Step 2: This exceeds the guaranteed ₹50,000, so there is NO deficiency and the guarantee is not used
Step 3: A's share = ₹3,60,000 × 3/6 = ₹1,80,000
Common mistake: Treating the ₹10,000 excess as a charge on A gives ₹1,70,000 (A). Deducting the whole guaranteed amount gives ₹1,30,000 (C). Adding C's excess to A gives ₹1,90,000 (D).
Key point: A guarantee is a floor, not a fixed amount — always check whether a deficiency actually arises.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Nature of partnership — essential elements
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an essential element of a partnership?
options: A) An agreement between the partners
B) The existence of a business
C) Sharing of the profits of the business
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Registration of the firm
Why: Registration under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 is optional. An unregistered firm is still a partnership, although it suffers some disabilities (for example, it cannot sue third parties to enforce a contract). The essential elements come from the definition in Section 4: an agreement, a business, profit sharing and mutual agency.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are all part of the legal definition of partnership.
Key point: Registration is desirable, not essential.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — finding capital employed from the super profit method
questions.question: A firm's goodwill, valued at three years' purchase of super profit, is ₹60,000. Its average profit is ₹1,00,000 and the normal rate of return is 10%. The firm's capital employed is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹8,00,000
Step 1: Super profit = Goodwill ÷ Years' purchase = ₹60,000 ÷ 3 = ₹20,000
Step 2: Normal profit = Average profit − Super profit = ₹1,00,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹80,000
Step 3: Capital employed = Normal profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate = ₹80,000 × 100/10 = ₹8,00,000
Common mistake: Capitalising the average profit gives ₹10,00,000 (B). ₹6,00,000 (C) does not follow from the data. Capitalising the super profit gives ₹2,00,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — premium when the share is taken from one partner
questions.question: A and B are partners. C is admitted for a 1/4th share, which he takes entirely from A. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,00,000, and C brings his share of goodwill in cash. The amount credited to A's Capital Account for goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹25,000
Step 1: C's share of goodwill = ₹1,00,000 × 1/4 = ₹25,000
Step 2: Only A sacrifices, so the whole premium is credited to A: Premium for Goodwill A/c Dr. ₹25,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹25,000
Common mistake: Splitting the premium equally gives ₹12,500 (A). ₹15,000 (B) assumes a 3 : 2 split. ₹1,00,000 (D) is the firm's total goodwill.
Key point: The premium goes to whoever sacrifices, in the ratio of their sacrifice.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Dissolution by the court
questions.question: Under Section 44 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, on which of the following grounds may the court dissolve a firm on the suit of a partner?
options: A) A partner has become of unsound mind
B) A new partner has been admitted
C) A partner has gone on a long holiday
D) The firm's profits have fallen in one year
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A partner has become of unsound mind
Why: Section 44 lists grounds for dissolution by the court, including a partner's unsound mind, permanent incapacity, misconduct, persistent breach of the agreement, transfer of his interest, the business being able to run only at a loss, and other just and equitable grounds.
Why not the others: (B) is reconstitution, not dissolution. (C) and (D) are not grounds for dissolution.
Key point: Court dissolution requires a serious, lasting problem, not a temporary setback.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of debentures — general principles
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the issue of debentures:
(A) Debenture Application and Debenture Allotment Accounts are used in the same way as for shares.
(B) If debentures are over-subscribed, the excess application money is refunded or adjusted.
(C) Debentures can be issued at a discount.
(D) Debenture holders receive dividend.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: The accounting for debentures follows that for shares — application and allotment accounts (A), and refund or adjustment of excess money (B). Unlike shares, debentures can be issued at a discount (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — debenture holders are creditors and receive INTEREST, not dividend. Options (A), (B) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: Shares → dividend (appropriation); debentures → interest (charge).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Unrecorded asset realised on dissolution
questions.question: On dissolution, the firm's goodwill, which was NOT recorded in the books, was sold for ₹15,000 in cash. The entry is:
options: A) Realisation A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Cash A/c ₹15,000
B) Cash A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Realisation A/c ₹15,000
C) Cash A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Partners' Capital A/cs ₹15,000
D) Goodwill A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Realisation A/c ₹15,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cash A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Realisation A/c ₹15,000
Why: An unrecorded asset has no book value on the debit side of the Realisation Account, so the whole amount realised is a gain, credited to the Realisation Account.
Why not the others:
(A) This is the entry for a PAYMENT.
(C) The gain reaches the partners only through the Realisation result.
(D) An unrecorded asset is not first brought into the books.
Key point: Unrecorded asset sold → Cash Dr.; To Realisation.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Over-subscription — excess beyond allotment kept as calls in advance
questions.question: A company offered 80,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, payable ₹4 on application, ₹3 on allotment and ₹3 on call. Applications were received for 1,60,000 shares, and all applicants were allotted shares pro-rata (none rejected). Excess application money was first adjusted towards allotment, and the balance was retained as calls in advance. The amount of calls in advance is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹80,000
Step 1: Application money received = 1,60,000 × ₹4 = ₹6,40,000; needed for 80,000 shares = ₹3,20,000 → excess = ₹3,20,000
Step 2: Allotment due = 80,000 × ₹3 = ₹2,40,000, fully covered by the excess
Step 3: Remaining excess = ₹3,20,000 − ₹2,40,000 = ₹80,000 → Calls in Advance A/c (adjusted when the call is made)
Common mistake: ₹3,20,000 (B) is the total excess. ₹2,40,000 (C) is the allotment covered. Nil (D) ignores the surplus.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Settlement of partners' balances on dissolution
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II on the dissolution of a firm:

List-I (Item)
(A) Debit balance in a solvent partner's Capital Account
(B) Credit balance in a partner's Capital Account
(C) A partner's loan to the firm
(D) Advertisement suspense (deferred revenue expenditure) appearing in the balance sheet

List-II (Treatment)
(I) Paid in cash before the partners' capitals
(II) Written off to the partners' Capital Accounts in their profit-sharing ratio
(III) The partner brings in cash
(IV) Paid to the partner in cash at the end

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why:
(A) A debit balance means the partner owes the firm, so he brings cash → (III).
(B) A credit balance is paid to the partner last → (IV).
(C) A partner's loan is paid after outsiders and before capital → (I).
(D) A fictitious item such as advertisement suspense has no realisable value, so it is written off to capitals → (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the debit and credit balances; (B) swaps the loan and the advertisement suspense; (D) swaps the debit balance and the loan.
Key point: Fictitious assets are never transferred to the Realisation A/c; they are written off to capitals.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — treatment of goodwill (AS-26)
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the treatment of goodwill on the retirement of a partner:
(A) Under AS-26, goodwill is not raised in the books on retirement.
(B) The retiring partner's share of goodwill is credited to his Capital Account.
(C) The remaining partners are debited in their gaining ratio.
(D) Goodwill is raised at its full value and retained in the books.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: AS-26 does not allow internally generated goodwill to be recognised (A). The retiring partner is compensated through the capital accounts: Remaining Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. (gaining ratio) (C); To Retiring Partner's Capital A/c (B).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — raising goodwill in the books contradicts AS-26. Options (A), (B) and (C) all include (D).
Key point: Retirement goodwill → a capital-account adjustment in the gaining ratio.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Share capital — preference shares
questions.question: Dividend on preference shares is:
options: B) Paid at a fixed rate
C) Paid only after equity dividend
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Paid at a fixed rate
Why: Preference shareholders are entitled to dividend at a FIXED rate (for example, 8% preference shares), and it is paid BEFORE any equity dividend.
Why not the others:
(A) describes equity dividend.
(C) Preference dividend is paid first.
(D) It is normally paid in cash.
Key point: Preference = fixed rate + priority; equity = variable + residual.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Realisation — creditor accepting an asset and others paid at a discount
questions.question: On dissolution: assets other than cash were ₹2,00,000 (including machinery of ₹40,000), and creditors were ₹80,000. One creditor of ₹30,000 accepted the machinery in full settlement, and the remaining creditors were paid in cash at a discount of 10%. The other assets realised ₹1,50,000. Realisation expenses of ₹2,000 were paid by partner A on behalf of the firm. The loss on realisation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹17,000
Step 1: The creditor who took the machinery needs no further entry (both items are already in the Realisation A/c)
Step 2: Remaining creditors ₹50,000 paid at 10% discount = ₹45,000 cash
Step 3: Debit side = Assets ₹2,00,000 + Cash to creditors ₹45,000 + Expenses (paid by A) ₹2,000 = ₹2,47,000
Step 4: Credit side = Creditors ₹80,000 + Cash from other assets ₹1,50,000 = ₹2,30,000
Step 5: Loss = ₹17,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the 10% discount gives ₹22,000 (A). Ignoring the expenses gives ₹15,000 (B). Also recording a ₹30,000 cash payment to the creditor who took the machinery gives ₹47,000, and other slips give ₹27,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Journal entries for issue of shares
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Event)
(A) Application money received
(B) Application money transferred on allotment
(C) Allotment money becomes due
(D) Call money received

List-II (Entry)
(I) Share Allotment A/c Dr.; To Share Capital A/c
(II) Bank A/c Dr.; To Share Call A/c
(III) Bank A/c Dr.; To Share Application A/c
(IV) Share Application A/c Dr.; To Share Capital A/c

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why:
(A) Cash received with applications → Bank Dr.; To Share Application (III).
(B) On allotment, the application money becomes share capital → Share Application Dr.; To Share Capital (IV).
(C) Allotment money due → Share Allotment Dr.; To Share Capital (I).
(D) Call money received → Bank Dr.; To Share Call (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps receipt and transfer; (B) swaps transfer and allotment; (C) swaps the two receipts.
Key point: Every instalment has a 'due' entry and a 'received' entry (for application, both happen at once).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — number of years' purchase
questions.question: A firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,20,000 on the basis of its average profit of ₹40,000. The number of years' purchase used is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3
Formula: Goodwill = Average profit × Number of years' purchase
Step 1: Number of years' purchase = ₹1,20,000 ÷ ₹40,000 = 3
Common mistake: 2 (A) and 4 (B) do not fit the data. Inverting the ratio gives 0.33 (D).
Key point: Years' purchase is the number of years for which the buyer is willing to pay for the profits.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Change in profit-sharing ratio — goodwill adjustment entry
questions.question: A, B and C share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1 and decide to share in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3 in future. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹90,000. The adjusting entry for goodwill is:
options: A) C's Capital A/c Dr. ₹30,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹30,000
B) A's Capital A/c Dr. ₹30,000; To C's Capital A/c ₹30,000
C) C's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To A's and B's Capital A/cs ₹7,500 each
D) B's Capital A/c Dr. ₹30,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹30,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) C's Capital A/c Dr. ₹30,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹30,000
Step 1: A: 3/6 − 1/6 = 2/6 sacrifice; B: 2/6 − 2/6 = no change; C: 1/6 − 3/6 = 2/6 gain
Step 2: Adjustment = ₹90,000 × 2/6 = ₹30,000, paid by C to A
Common mistake: Reversing the entry gives (B). Spreading the adjustment over A and B gives (C), but B's share is unchanged. (D) debits B, who neither gains nor sacrifices.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — total amount due to the retiring partner
questions.question: A, B and C share profits equally. B retires. His capital is ₹80,000. The balance sheet shows a General Reserve of ₹30,000 and a debit balance of ₹6,000 in the Profit and Loss Account. B's share of goodwill is ₹18,000, and the revaluation shows a profit of ₹9,000. The total amount due to B is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹1,09,000
Step 1: Capital = ₹80,000
Step 2: General Reserve (1/3 of ₹30,000) = +₹10,000
Step 3: Accumulated loss (1/3 of ₹6,000) = −₹2,000
Step 4: Goodwill = +₹18,000
Step 5: Revaluation profit (1/3 of ₹9,000) = +₹3,000
Step 6: Amount due = 80,000 + 10,000 − 2,000 + 18,000 + 3,000 = ₹1,09,000
Common mistake: Adding the P&L debit balance gives ₹1,13,000 (B). Leaving out goodwill gives ₹91,000 (C). Treating the revaluation profit as a loss gives ₹1,03,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Premium payable with the call money
questions.question: A company issued 10,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2. The premium is payable with the first and final call of ₹5 per share. The amount credited to the Securities Premium Account when the call is made is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹20,000
Step 1: Call money ₹5 per share = ₹3 towards capital + ₹2 premium
Step 2: Securities Premium = 10,000 × ₹2 = ₹20,000
Entry: Share First and Final Call A/c Dr. ₹50,000; To Share Capital A/c ₹30,000; To Securities Premium A/c ₹20,000
Common mistake: ₹50,000 (A) is the total call money. ₹30,000 (B) is the capital part. ₹10,000 (C) assumes a premium of ₹1.
Key point: The premium is credited in whichever instalment it is payable.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — transfer of the revaluation balance
questions.question: On the admission of a partner, the balance of the Revaluation Account is transferred to:
options: A) All the partners, including the new partner, in the new ratio
C) The partners in their sacrificing ratio
D) The old partners' Capital Accounts in their old ratio
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The old partners' Capital Accounts in their old ratio
Why: The revaluation gain or loss arose before the admission, while only the old partners owned the firm, so it is shared by them in the old ratio.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) wrongly include the new partner. (C) The sacrificing ratio is used only for goodwill.
Key point: Revaluation balance → old partners, old ratio.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on capital — partner admitted during the year
questions.question: C was admitted as a partner on 1 October 2025 and brought ₹1,00,000 as capital. Interest on capital is allowed at 10% p.a., and the books are closed on 31 March 2026. Interest on C's capital for the year is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹5,000
Step 1: C's capital was used from 1 October 2025 to 31 March 2026 = 6 months
Step 2: Interest = ₹1,00,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₹5,000
Common mistake: Charging a full year gives ₹10,000 (B). Using 3 months gives ₹2,500 (C). Using 9 months gives ₹7,500 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — new ratio of continuing partners
questions.question:
Assertion (A): After the retirement of a partner, the continuing partners always share future profits in their old ratio.
Reason (R): The continuing partners are free to agree on any new profit-sharing ratio.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
Why: Partners can agree on any ratio for the reconstituted firm (the Reason is true). Their old ratio continues only if they acquire the retiring partner's share in that ratio or say nothing about it. So the word 'always' makes the Assertion false.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) treat the Assertion as true.
Key point: New ratio = old share + share acquired; the acquisition may be in any agreed proportion.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on drawings — monthly drawings for part of the year
questions.question: Gopal joined the firm's drawings scheme only in the second half of the year: he drew ₹5,000 on the first day of every month from 1 October 2025 to 1 March 2026 (six drawings). The firm charges 12% p.a. on drawings and closes its books on 31 March 2026. What is the interest on Gopal's drawings?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,050
Given: Total drawings = 6 × ₹5,000 = ₹30,000, each at the beginning of the month.
Step 1: The first drawing (1 October) earns interest for 6 months and the last (1 March) for 1 month → average period = (6 + 1) ÷ 2 = 3.5 months
Step 2: Interest = ₹30,000 × 12% × 3.5/12 = ₹1,050
Common mistake: Using 6 months gives ₹1,800 (A). Treating the drawings as made at the END of each month (average 2.5 months) gives ₹750 (C). Charging a full year gives ₹3,600 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — settlement for less than the amount due
questions.question: On C's retirement, the amount due to him is ₹1,00,000. He agrees to accept ₹90,000 in full settlement. The continuing partners A and B have a gaining ratio of 3 : 2. The amount credited to A's Capital Account on this settlement is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹6,000
Why: By accepting less, C gives up ₹10,000 of his claim. This benefit goes to the continuing partners who acquire his share, in their gaining ratio.
Step 1: C's Capital A/c Dr. ₹1,00,000; To Bank A/c ₹90,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹6,000; To B's Capital A/c ₹4,000
Step 2: A's credit = ₹10,000 × 3/5 = ₹6,000
Common mistake: ₹10,000 (A) is the total benefit. Splitting it equally gives ₹5,000 (B). ₹4,000 (D) is B's share.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Past adjustments — profits of several years in the wrong ratio
questions.question: The profits of A and B for the last three years — ₹60,000, ₹80,000 and ₹1,00,000 — were distributed in the ratio 3 : 2, although the deed provides for equal sharing. Their capitals are fixed. The single adjusting entry to correct all three years is:
options: A) B's Current A/c Dr. ₹24,000; To A's Current A/c ₹24,000
B) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹48,000; To B's Current A/c ₹48,000
C) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹24,000; To B's Current A/c ₹24,000
D) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To B's Current A/c ₹10,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹24,000; To B's Current A/c ₹24,000
Step 1: Total profit = ₹60,000 + ₹80,000 + ₹1,00,000 = ₹2,40,000
Step 2: Actually credited (3 : 2): A ₹1,44,000; B ₹96,000
Step 3: Correct (1 : 1): A ₹1,20,000; B ₹1,20,000
Step 4: A was over-credited by ₹24,000 → A's Current A/c Dr. ₹24,000; To B's Current A/c ₹24,000
Common mistake: Reversing the entry gives (A). Doubling the difference gives ₹48,000 (B). Correcting only the latest year gives ₹10,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Calls in arrears — interest on two instalments
questions.question: A company follows Table F (interest on calls in arrears at 10% p.a.). A shareholder paid his overdue allotment money of ₹6,000 three months late and his overdue call money of ₹4,000 six months late. The total interest charged on calls in arrears is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹350
Step 1: On allotment arrears: ₹6,000 × 10% × 3/12 = ₹150
Step 2: On call arrears: ₹4,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₹200
Step 3: Total = ₹350
Common mistake: Using 12% (the calls-in-advance rate) gives ₹420 (B). Charging a full year on both gives ₹1,000 (C). Using 3 months for both gives ₹250 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Change in profit-sharing ratio — existing goodwill and new goodwill
questions.question: A and B share profits equally. They decide to share in the ratio 2 : 1 in future. Goodwill already appears in the books at ₹40,000 and is to be written off. The goodwill is now valued at ₹1,20,000 and adjusted through the capital accounts. The net effect of these goodwill entries on B's Capital Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) No change
Step 1: Write off the existing goodwill in the old ratio 1 : 1 → B is debited ₹20,000
Step 2: Change in shares: A = 2/3 − 1/2 = 1/6 gain; B = 1/3 − 1/2 = 1/6 sacrifice
Step 3: Adjustment = ₹1,20,000 × 1/6 = ₹20,000 → A's Capital A/c Dr.; To B's Capital A/c ₹20,000 → B is credited ₹20,000
Step 4: Net effect on B = −₹20,000 + ₹20,000 = nil
Common mistake: Counting only the write-off gives a decrease of ₹20,000 (A). Counting only the adjustment gives an increase of ₹20,000 (C). Doubling the adjustment gives (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — old partners change their mutual ratio
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 3 : 1. They admit C for a 1/4th share and, at the same time, agree that they will share the remaining profits between themselves in the ratio 2 : 1. The new profit-sharing ratio of A, B and C is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2 : 1 : 1
Step 1: C's share = 1/4; remaining share for A and B = 3/4
Step 2: A and B divide the 3/4 in their NEW mutual ratio 2 : 1 → A = 3/4 × 2/3 = 2/4; B = 3/4 × 1/3 = 1/4
Step 3: New ratio A : B : C = 2/4 : 1/4 : 1/4 = 2 : 1 : 1
Check: A's sacrifice = 3/4 − 2/4 = 1/4; B's = 1/4 − 1/4 = 0 → C's share comes entirely from A.
Common mistake: Dividing the remaining 3/4 in the OLD ratio 3 : 1 gives 9/16 : 3/16 : 4/16 = 9 : 3 : 4 (A). 3 : 1 : 1 (C) and 1 : 1 : 1 (D) do not follow the agreed ratios.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Charges against profit — partner's loan and rent
questions.question: A firm's profit before charging interest on a partner's loan and rent to a partner is ₹1,00,000. Partner B has lent ₹50,000 to the firm, and the deed is silent on interest on loans. Partner A has let his premises to the firm at a rent of ₹1,000 per month. The profit available for distribution among the partners is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹85,000
Step 1: Interest on B's loan at 6% p.a. (Section 13(d), as the deed is silent) = ₹50,000 × 6% = ₹3,000 — a charge
Step 2: Rent to A = ₹1,000 × 12 = ₹12,000 — a charge (A acts as a landlord, not as a partner)
Step 3: Divisible profit = ₹1,00,000 − ₹3,000 − ₹12,000 = ₹85,000
Common mistake: Charging loan interest at 10% gives ₹83,000 (B). Leaving out the rent gives ₹97,000 (C). Ignoring both charges gives ₹1,00,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Over-subscription — application money received
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Kavya Ltd. invited applications for 60,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at par, payable ₹2 on application, ₹3 on allotment and ₹5 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 90,000 shares, and shares were allotted as follows: applicants for 40,000 shares were allotted 30,000 shares, and applicants for 50,000 shares were allotted 30,000 shares. Excess application money was adjusted towards the allotment money. Meera, who had applied for 1,000 shares in the second category, failed to pay the allotment and the call money. Her shares were forfeited after the call. The forfeited shares were later re-issued at ₹11 per share as fully paid.

Question: The total application money received by the company is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,80,000
Step 1: Applications received for 90,000 shares × ₹2 = ₹1,80,000 (all of it is received, even though some is later adjusted)
Common mistake: Counting only the 60,000 shares offered gives ₹1,20,000 (A). ₹60,000 (C) is the total excess. Using ₹3 per share gives ₹2,70,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Pro-rata allotment in categories — excess adjusted
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Kavya Ltd. invited applications for 60,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at par, payable ₹2 on application, ₹3 on allotment and ₹5 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 90,000 shares, and shares were allotted as follows: applicants for 40,000 shares were allotted 30,000 shares, and applicants for 50,000 shares were allotted 30,000 shares. Excess application money was adjusted towards the allotment money. Meera, who had applied for 1,000 shares in the second category, failed to pay the allotment and the call money. Her shares were forfeited after the call. The forfeited shares were later re-issued at ₹11 per share as fully paid.

Question: How much of the second category's application money becomes surplus and is carried forward to the allotment stage?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹40,000
Step 1: Second category applied for 50,000 shares and was allotted 30,000 → excess 20,000 shares
Step 2: Excess money = 20,000 × ₹2 = ₹40,000; allotment due on 30,000 shares = ₹90,000, so the whole ₹40,000 can be adjusted
Common mistake: ₹20,000 (A) is the first category's excess (10,000 × ₹2). ₹60,000 (B) is the total of both categories. ₹1,00,000 (C) is the second category's entire application money.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Pro-rata allotment — individual shareholder
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Kavya Ltd. invited applications for 60,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at par, payable ₹2 on application, ₹3 on allotment and ₹5 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 90,000 shares, and shares were allotted as follows: applicants for 40,000 shares were allotted 30,000 shares, and applicants for 50,000 shares were allotted 30,000 shares. Excess application money was adjusted towards the allotment money. Meera, who had applied for 1,000 shares in the second category, failed to pay the allotment and the call money. Her shares were forfeited after the call. The forfeited shares were later re-issued at ₹11 per share as fully paid.

Question: Meera receives how many shares, and what amount remains outstanding from her when the allotment money falls due?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 600 shares; ₹1,000
Step 1: Second-category ratio = 50,000 : 30,000 = 5 : 3 → Meera gets 1,000 × 3/5 = 600 shares
Step 2: Application money paid = 1,000 × ₹2 = ₹2,000; needed for 600 shares = ₹1,200; excess = ₹800
Step 3: Allotment due = 600 × ₹3 = ₹1,800; less excess ₹800 = ₹1,000 unpaid
Common mistake: Applying the first category's ratio (4 : 3) gives 750 shares and ₹1,750 (B). Ignoring the excess gives ₹1,800 (C). Allotting in full gives (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Forfeiture of a pro-rata allottee's shares
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Kavya Ltd. invited applications for 60,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at par, payable ₹2 on application, ₹3 on allotment and ₹5 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 90,000 shares, and shares were allotted as follows: applicants for 40,000 shares were allotted 30,000 shares, and applicants for 50,000 shares were allotted 30,000 shares. Excess application money was adjusted towards the allotment money. Meera, who had applied for 1,000 shares in the second category, failed to pay the allotment and the call money. Her shares were forfeited after the call. The forfeited shares were later re-issued at ₹11 per share as fully paid.

Question: The amount credited to the Share Forfeiture Account on forfeiture of Meera's shares is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹2,000
Step 1: Share Capital A/c Dr. = 600 × ₹10 = ₹6,000
Step 2: Unpaid amounts: allotment ₹1,000; call 600 × ₹5 = ₹3,000; total ₹4,000
Step 3: Share Forfeiture A/c Cr. = ₹6,000 − ₹4,000 = ₹2,000 — that is, ALL the money Meera actually paid (₹1,200 application + ₹800 excess used on allotment)
Common mistake: Counting only the application money on 600 shares gives ₹1,200 (A). ₹4,000 (B) is the unpaid amount. ₹6,000 (D) is the called-up capital.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Re-issue of forfeited shares at a premium
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

Kavya Ltd. invited applications for 60,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at par, payable ₹2 on application, ₹3 on allotment and ₹5 on the first and final call. Applications were received for 90,000 shares, and shares were allotted as follows: applicants for 40,000 shares were allotted 30,000 shares, and applicants for 50,000 shares were allotted 30,000 shares. Excess application money was adjusted towards the allotment money. Meera, who had applied for 1,000 shares in the second category, failed to pay the allotment and the call money. Her shares were forfeited after the call. The forfeited shares were later re-issued at ₹11 per share as fully paid.

Question: On the re-issue of Meera's shares, the amounts credited to Securities Premium and transferred to Capital Reserve are:
options: A) Securities Premium nil; Capital Reserve ₹2,600
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Securities Premium ₹600; Capital Reserve ₹2,000
Step 1: Re-issue price ₹11 = face value ₹10 + premium ₹1 → Securities Premium = 600 × ₹1 = ₹600
Step 2: There is no discount, so nothing is debited to Share Forfeiture
Step 3: The whole forfeited amount of ₹2,000 is a capital profit → Capital Reserve ₹2,000
Common mistake: Adding the premium to Capital Reserve gives (A). Deducting the premium from the forfeited amount gives (C). Swapping the two amounts gives (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Accounting ratios — limitations
questions.question:
Which of the following are limitations of ratio analysis?
(A) Different accounting policies across firms can distort comparisons.
(B) Ratios ignore changes in the price level.
(C) Ratios are a means, not an end, and need careful interpretation.
(D) Ratios alone give a complete picture of a business.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Comparisons are only valid when accounting methods are similar (A). Historical-cost figures ignore inflation (B). And ratios are only indicators that must be interpreted along with other information (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — ratios ignore qualitative factors and give only a partial picture. Options (A), (B) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: Ratios point to questions; they do not answer them on their own.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Liquidity ratios — effect of a credit purchase
questions.question: A company's current assets are ₹2,00,000 and its current liabilities ₹1,00,000. It then purchases goods worth ₹20,000 on credit. Its new current ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.83 : 1
Step 1: A credit purchase increases BOTH current assets (inventory) and current liabilities (creditors) by ₹20,000
Step 2: New current ratio = ₹2,20,000 ÷ ₹1,20,000 = 1.83 : 1
Common mistake: Assuming no change gives 2 : 1 (A). Increasing only the current assets gives 2.2 : 1 (B). Increasing only the liabilities gives 1.67 : 1 (D).
Key point: When the current ratio is above 1, an equal increase in both current assets and current liabilities lowers it.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from financing activities — preference shares and interim dividend
questions.question: During the year a company: issued equity shares of ₹3,00,000 at par; redeemed 10% preference shares of ₹1,00,000 at a premium of 5%; raised a long-term loan of ₹50,000; paid interest on the loan of ₹6,000; and paid an interim dividend of ₹20,000. The net cash flow from financing activities is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹2,19,000 inflow
Step 1: Inflows = Shares ₹3,00,000 + Loan ₹50,000 = ₹3,50,000
Step 2: Outflows = Redemption ₹1,05,000 (including premium) + Interest ₹6,000 + Interim dividend ₹20,000 = ₹1,31,000
Step 3: Net = ₹3,50,000 − ₹1,31,000 = ₹2,19,000 inflow
Common mistake: Redeeming at par gives ₹2,24,000 (A). Leaving out the interest and dividend gives ₹2,45,000 (B). Leaving out the new loan gives ₹1,69,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Financial analysis — users and their focus
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (User)
(A) Short-term creditors
(B) Long-term lenders
(C) Shareholders
(D) Management

List-II (Main focus of analysis)
(I) Overall operational efficiency and control
(II) Liquidity
(III) Long-term solvency
(IV) Profitability and returns

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why:
(A) Short-term creditors want to be paid soon → liquidity (II).
(B) Long-term lenders want interest and repayment over years → solvency (III).
(C) Shareholders want returns and dividends → profitability (IV).
(D) Management needs to evaluate and control the whole business → efficiency (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the two creditor groups; (C) swaps lenders and shareholders; (D) swaps creditors and management.
Key point: Each user picks the ratios that match his own stake.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Liquidity ratios — finding inventory
questions.question: A company's current ratio is 2 : 1 and its quick ratio is 1.2 : 1. Its current liabilities are ₹50,000 and its prepaid expenses are ₹5,000. Its inventory is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹35,000
Step 1: Current assets = 2 × ₹50,000 = ₹1,00,000
Step 2: Quick assets = 1.2 × ₹50,000 = ₹60,000
Step 3: Current assets − Quick assets = Inventory + Prepaid expenses = ₹40,000
Step 4: Inventory = ₹40,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹35,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the prepaid expenses gives ₹40,000 (B). Adding them gives ₹45,000 (C). ₹60,000 (D) is the quick assets.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Activity ratios — inventory turnover (working back to revenue)
questions.question: A company's inventory turnover ratio is 6 times and its average inventory is ₹75,000. Its gross profit is 25% of revenue from operations. Its revenue from operations is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹6,00,000
Step 1: Cost of revenue = Turnover × Average inventory = 6 × ₹75,000 = ₹4,50,000
Step 2: Gross profit is 25% of revenue, so cost of revenue = 75% of revenue
Step 3: Revenue = ₹4,50,000 ÷ 0.75 = ₹6,00,000
Common mistake: Treating 25% as a margin on COST gives ₹4,50,000 × 1.25 = ₹5,62,500 (B). ₹4,50,000 (C) is the cost of revenue. ₹5,00,000 (D) does not follow from the data.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from operating activities — working capital items and tax
questions.question: Operating profit before working capital changes is ₹1,50,000. During the year: inventory decreased by ₹10,000; prepaid expenses increased by ₹2,000; outstanding expenses decreased by ₹3,000; and income tax of ₹25,000 was paid. Net cash from operating activities is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,30,000
Step 1: Decrease in inventory releases cash → +₹10,000
Step 2: Increase in prepaid expenses uses cash → −₹2,000
Step 3: Decrease in outstanding expenses means more was paid → −₹3,000
Step 4: Cash generated = 1,50,000 + 10,000 − 2,000 − 3,000 = ₹1,55,000; less tax ₹25,000 → ₹1,30,000
Common mistake: Stopping before tax gives ₹1,55,000 (A). Reversing the signs of the prepaid and outstanding expenses gives ₹1,40,000 (B). Deducting the fall in inventory gives ₹1,10,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Tools of financial analysis
questions.question: An analyst studying a company's published statements uses several techniques. Which one of the following is NOT a technique of analysing financial statements?
options: D) Preparation of the trial balance
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Preparation of the trial balance
Why: The trial balance is a step in the accounting process that checks arithmetical accuracy BEFORE the financial statements are prepared. Analysis tools work on the finished statements: comparative and common-size statements, trend analysis, ratio analysis and the cash flow statement.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are standard tools of analysis.
Key point: Accounting process → statements → analysis.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Solvency ratios — effect of a transaction on debt-equity ratio
questions.question: Issue of debentures for cash will have which effect on a company's debt-equity ratio?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Increase
Why: Debentures are long-term debt. Issuing them for cash raises the numerator (debt), while shareholders' funds (the denominator) stay the same, so the ratio rises.
Why not the others:
(A) This would follow from repaying debt or issuing shares.
(C) The debt changes, so the ratio cannot stay the same.
(D) It becomes nil only if there is no debt at all.
Key point: More debt → higher D/E → more financial risk.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Financial statements of a company — Schedule III headings
questions.question: As per Schedule III, 'Trade marks' owned by a company are shown in the balance sheet under:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Intangible assets
Why: Trade marks are non-physical, long-lived rights, so Schedule III places them under Non-current assets — Intangible assets, along with goodwill, patents, copyrights and computer software.
Why not the others:
(B) Inventories are goods held for sale or production.
(C) Other current assets are short-term items.
(D) Investments are holdings in other entities.
Key point: Intangible assets include goodwill, brands and trade marks, patents and software.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll accounting — cost to the employer
questions.question: An employee's basic pay is ₹20,000 per month. DA is 50% of basic pay and HRA is 10% of basic pay. The employer contributes 12% of (basic pay + DA) to the Provident Fund. The monthly cost of this employee to the employer (CTC) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹35,600
Step 1: DA = 50% × ₹20,000 = ₹10,000; HRA = 10% × ₹20,000 = ₹2,000 → gross salary = ₹32,000
Step 2: Employer's PF = 12% × (₹20,000 + ₹10,000) = ₹3,600
Step 3: Cost to the employer = ₹32,000 + ₹3,600 = ₹35,600
Common mistake: ₹32,000 (A) is the gross salary only. Deducting PF instead of adding it gives ₹28,400 (B). Calculating PF on the gross salary gives ₹35,840 (C).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Accounting Information System — components
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Component of AIS)
(A) Hardware
(B) Software
(C) People
(D) Procedures and instructions

List-II (Description)
(I) Computers, servers and networking devices
(II) Programs that process the accounting data
(III) Users who enter, operate and use the system
(IV) Methods for collecting, storing and processing data

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Hardware is the physical equipment → (I).
(B) Software is the programs → (II).
(C) People are the users → (III).
(D) Procedures are the methods followed → (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps hardware and software; (C) swaps people and procedures; (D) swaps hardware and people.
Key point: AIS = people + procedures + data + software + IT infrastructure + internal controls.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — SUM function
questions.question: Which formula correctly adds the values in cells A1 to A10?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) =SUM(A1:A10)
Why: SUM takes a range written as first cell:last cell. A1:A10 includes all ten cells.
Why not the others:
(A) ADD is not a spreadsheet function (it gives #NAME?).
(B) A1+A10 adds only two cells.
(C) TOTAL is not a standard function, and the separator is wrong.
Key point: A colon (:) means a range; a plus sign (+) adds only the cells named.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — operator precedence in a formula
questions.question: The value returned by the formula =2+3*4^2 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 50
Step 1: Exponent first: 4^2 = 16
Step 2: Then multiplication: 3 × 16 = 48
Step 3: Then addition: 2 + 48 = 50
Common mistake: Working strictly left to right ((2 + 3) × 4 = 20, then 20² = 400) gives 400 (B). Squaring (3 × 4) gives 2 + 144 = 146 (C). Squaring (2 + 3 × 4) gives 196 (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — COUNT versus COUNTA
questions.question: A column of a ledger extract has six cells, A1 to A6, holding: 10, Cash, 20, an empty cell, 30 and Nil. How many cells does =COUNT(A1:A6) count?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3
Why: COUNT counts only cells that contain NUMBERS — here 10, 20 and 30. Text ('Cash', 'Nil') and blank cells are ignored.
Why not the others:
(A) 6 counts every cell.
(B) 5 counts all non-blank cells, which is what =COUNTA gives.
(D) 2 has no basis.
Key point: COUNT → numbers only; COUNTA → anything that is not blank.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — order of operations
questions.question: In a spreadsheet formula, which of the following operators is evaluated FIRST?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ^ (exponentiation)
Why: Spreadsheets follow this order of precedence: brackets → exponent (^) → multiplication and division (* /) → addition and subtraction (+ −). Operators of equal precedence are evaluated from left to right.
Why not the others: (C) * comes after ^; (A) and (D) come last.
Key point: Use brackets whenever you want a different order.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Generating accounting information — IF for outstanding invoices
questions.question: In a receivables sheet, the outstanding amount is calculated with =IF(B2="Paid",0,C2). If B2 contains Due and C2 contains 5000, the formula returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 5000
Step 1: Condition: is B2 equal to 'Paid'? It contains 'Due' → FALSE
Step 2: The FALSE part returns C2 → 5000 (the amount still outstanding)
Common mistake: 0 (A) would be returned only for a paid invoice. 'Paid' (B) and 'Due' (D) are text that this formula never returns.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Depreciation schedule — two assets
questions.question: A depreciation schedule uses =SLN for two assets. Asset 1 cost ₹1,00,000, has a life of 5 years and no salvage value, and was bought at the start of Year 1. Asset 2 cost ₹60,000, has a life of 4 years and a salvage value of ₹4,000, and was bought at the start of Year 2. The total depreciation charged in Year 2 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹34,000
Step 1: Asset 1: =SLN(100000,0,5) = ₹20,000 per year
Step 2: Asset 2: =SLN(60000,4000,4) = ₹56,000 ÷ 4 = ₹14,000 per year (it is used for the whole of Year 2)
Step 3: Total for Year 2 = ₹20,000 + ₹14,000 = ₹34,000
Common mistake: Ignoring Asset 2's salvage value gives ₹35,000 (A). Leaving out Asset 2 gives ₹20,000 (C). Using a 5-year life for Asset 2 (₹11,200) gives ₹31,200 (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Features of CAS — reporting
questions.question: A manager can obtain a trial balance or a profit and loss statement for ANY chosen period at any moment. This is possible because of which feature of a computerised accounting system?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Real-time, on-demand reporting
Why: In CAS, every voucher updates the database instantly. Reports are generated from the current data whenever they are needed, for any date range, without waiting for month-end closing.
Why not the others:
(B) Codification organises the accounts.
(C) Back-up protects the data.
(D) An audit trail records changes.
Key point: Data entered once → reports for any period, instantly.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Structure of CAS — chart of accounts
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the chart of accounts in a computerised accounting system:
(A) It lists all the accounts used by the business, with their codes.
(B) Accounts in it are arranged in a hierarchy of groups.
(C) It helps in preparing financial statements and reports.
(D) It is a graphical chart showing trends in account balances.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: The chart of accounts is the structured list of all ledger accounts with their codes (A), arranged in groups and sub-groups (B). Because every transaction is classified through it, reports and statements follow automatically (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — despite the word 'chart', it is a LIST, not a graph. Options (A), (B) and (C) all include (D).
Key point: Chart of accounts = coded master list of accounts.
